description: We are a team driven by a shared interest in science, technology, and space exploration. Combining our curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills, we set out to transform a complex lunar mission-planning challenge into an accessible and practical tool. Throughout the development of LUNA, we brought together scientific research, engineering concepts, software development, and data visualization, working collaboratively to turn real scientific data into meaningful interactive experiences.
summary:
LUNA (Lunar Utility for Navigation and Assessment) is an interactive, bilingual web application designed to make lunar exploration and landing-site evaluation more accessible, intuitive, and efficient. By integrating NASA and other scientific datasets, LUNA allows users to explore the Moon through interactive 2D and 3D maps, visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth at any selected location and time, assess sunlight and communication conditions, and analyze terrain and local gravity. It also features a timeline simulation and automated tools for evaluating landing feasibility.

LUNA consolidates complex scientific data and mission-planning capabilities into a single platform, eliminating the need to navigate multiple specialized tools. Users can compare up to six landing sites simultaneously, perform an area search to identify optimal landing locations, visualize lunar surface suitability through a global heat map, and evaluate spacecraft descent feasibility based on available fuel and orbital conditions.

Beyond supporting future lunar exploration, LUNA makes space science more accessible through its bilingual interface and optional educational features. It promotes inclusive STEM education, contributing to UN SDG 4 (Quality Education), while aligning with the United Nations General-Secretary's vision of an open, accessible, and inclusive cyberspace. Ultimately, LUNA brings space discovery, scientific innovation and educational opportunities closer to everyone.
details:
Our Project

LUNA lets anyone explore a detailed, navigable map of the Moon, visit the places where spacecraft have landed, and ask the questions a mission planner would ask about any point of the surface: Where will the Sun and the Earth be in the sky at this place and time? How long will the daylight last? Is the ground a crater? How strong is gravity here? Which is the best place to land inside this region? Can my spacecraft reach it with the fuel it has? Every answer is computed from real data and real physics, and the application says how reliable each number is.

What does it do?

  • Explore the Moon: The application features both a 2D and 3D map, allowing users to switch between a flat map and a rotating globe with terrain relief through a smooth transition that preserves the currently viewed location. It incorporates real lunar imagery at multiple levels of detail, covering the entire Moon at 100 meters per pixel using data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, providing approximately 20 meters per pixel resolution through Japan's Kaguya orbiter, and offering 39 high-resolution regions at approximately 0.5–1 meter per pixel, including the Apollo landing sites. As users zoom in, additional details load progressively, similarly to modern mapping applications. The application also includes 2,023 officially named lunar features, such as craters, maria, mountains, and valleys, based on the International Astronomical Union's catalogue, which can be searched by name or located by entering coordinates. Finally, it features a realistic celestial background displaying 8,404 catalogued stars in their actual positions, alongside the Sun and Earth at their corresponding locations during the simulated moment.
  • Plan a landing at any point and time: The application provides detailed information about the Sun, including its elevation above the local horizon, direction, time remaining until sunrise or sunset, and the duration of continuous daylight. It also displays information about the Earth, such as its elevation, visibility from the selected location (which is essential for establishing direct radio communication), its current phase, and whether it periodically rises and sets or remains continuously visible. To facilitate visualization, the application includes angle diagrams, a sky panorama showing the positions of the Sun and Earth, and an interactive 30-day timeline that can be dragged or played like a film to observe the progression of a lunar day. Additionally, it incorporates a terrain-screening tool called Crater Checker, which compares the elevation of a selected point with the surrounding terrain to identify whether it is located within a depression. This feature allows users to adjust the analysis radius and visualize the selected area directly on the map. Finally, the application calculates local gravitational acceleration in m/s² for the exact selected location using NASA's GRAIL gravity measurements.
  • Compare and decide: The application includes a site-comparison tool that allows users to evaluate up to six landing locations simultaneously under the same lunar conditions. It compares simple criteria, such as whether the Sun is above the horizon, the presence of low-angle sunlight, the remaining daylight hours, and Earth visibility, highlighting the most favourable location. It also features an area-search function that allows users to draw a rectangle directly on the map, within which the application evaluates thousands of potential landing points and recommends the most suitable location, providing an overall score, explanations for its selection, and alternative candidates. Additionally, a suitability heat map can be generated to visualize the entire lunar surface according to its landing conditions at a selected time. The heat map also updates according to the selected landing time, allowing users to observe how favourable landing regions shift across the lunar surface. Finally, the initial-conditions tool allows users to describe a spacecraft by specifying its position, altitude, velocity, mass, and available propellant. Based on these parameters, the application can identify the most suitable landing site within the spacecraft's reach or calculate the required velocity change (Δv) to reach a selected destination.
  • Learn while exploring: The application also includes a "Curious Mind" mode, which provides brief explanations alongside technical terminology, informational fact sheets for each historical lunar site, and interactive "Did you know…?" cards containing interesting facts about the Moon and its exploration. When this mode is disabled, the interface maintains a purely technical presentation, without additional educational explanations. Furthermore, the entire application is available in both English and Spanish, allowing users to switch between languages at any time without affecting their current session or progress.

How does it works?

LUNA is a single-page web application where everything is calculated in the user's browser without server-side computation. While imagery is streamed from NASA's public Moon Trek service, the elevation model, gravity field, star catalogue, and place names are bundled with the application for a total of 9.7 MB, allowing the planner, terrain analysis, and search to continue working offline. Its architecture splits the code into independent systems that communicate exclusively through a central application state, meaning the map and the planner read the same state and cannot disagree. The map engine utilizes a custom WebGL renderer for tiled imagery, 2D and 3D views, relief, picking, markers, overlays, and a star field. The lunar data layer handles the landing-site registry, imagery sources, elevation grid, place names, star catalogue, and mission icons. The astronomical engine calculates the positions and rise and set predictions of the Sun and Earth as seen from any point on the Moon. The simulation engine manages the simulated clock through scrubbing, playback, and animated time jumps, while the terrain analysis handles the Crater Checker and local gravity. Furthermore, the comparison engine provides criteria and ranking for several sites at once, the area optimiser runs candidate generation, filtering, and scoring in a background Web Worker thread, and the heat map executes whole-Moon scoring in its own background thread with cached terrain analysis. Finally, the descent guidance computes orbital mechanics for the initial-conditions tool and its trajectory line, and the user interface encompasses the sidebar, planner, toolbar, panels, and translations.

Benefits

LUNA consolidates complex tools for maps, ephemerides, elevation, gravity, and orbital mechanics into a single, free, browser-based interface built on public data and open-source libraries, allowing users to simply click any point on a map for instant answers. Delivering reliable data validated against NASA/JPL’s reference system, the platform transparently tags every value as measured, calculated, or approximate while clearly stating the limits of its analyses. Its responsive engine ensures fast feedback without freezing the screen—updating the Sun, Earth, countdowns, and map immediately as you drag the timeline, completing area searches in about a second, and rendering initial whole-Moon heat maps in roughly half a second. Designed to serve both novices and experts, it features a "Curious mind" toggle that switches between plain-language explanations and a compact technical instrument, while offering seamless English and Spanish support from a single codebase. Finally, its modular architecture is built to grow, letting developers add new landing sites, image layers, scoring criteria, map tools, or languages simply by adding data or small modules without having to rewrite the core system.

Intended impact

As humanity returns to the Moon, LUNA makes the rarely explained factors behind lunar landing decisions—such as sunlight for power and visibility, line of sight to Earth for communication, safe terrain, and landing fuel—accessible for anyone to explore firsthand. For education and outreach, it gives students, teachers, and the public a hands-on way to manipulate time and location to see why a lunar day lasts two weeks, why Earth hangs nearly still in the sky, why Apollo crews landed with a low Sun, and why the far side requires a relay satellite, while even letting users virtually stand at Apollo 11 or Chandrayaan-3 landing sites to view the sky as it appeared at those historic moments. It also supports early-stage analysis by giving enthusiasts and small teams a rapid first look at candidate landing sites—evaluating lighting, Earth visibility, terrain, and reachability—before moving on to professional tools. With a complete Spanish interface just one click away from the English default, the platform ensures broad accessibility, all built upon a modular, reusable foundation ready to support future capabilities like rover routes, shadow analysis, resource maps, and full landing trajectories.

Tools used

For programming languages, TypeScript is used for the application and tests, while GLSL handles the graphics shaders for the Moon, stars, and Earth. CSS and HTML build the interface, JavaScript on Node.js handles data-preparation scripts, and a little Python is used for checking images during development.

React 19 serves as the interface framework. For 3D graphics, the application utilizes WebGL 2 through three.js 0.187, featuring a custom tile renderer and shaders written specifically for the project without any ready-made map library.

The astronomy stack relies on astronomy-engine 2.1 for planetary and lunar positions, alongside a custom implementation for the Moon's orientation, the observer's sky, and rise/set prediction. Zustand 5 is used to manage the application state.

Build and testing operations are handled by Vite 8 as the build tool, Vitest 5 for automated tests, TypeScript 7 compiler for type checking, Node.js 26, and npm. The design incorporates Nunito and JetBrains Mono fonts alongside Lucide icons.

Background computing leverages Web Workers, which are browser threads dedicated to the area search and the heat map. Browser testing is automated using Microsoft Edge driven by Playwright to exercise each feature and capture screenshots for the document.

External services include NASA Moon Trek for map tiles, the NASA Planetary Data System for elevation and gravity data, NASA/JPL Horizons for reference values for validation, and the USGS/IAU gazetteer. Furthermore, the code was written and tested with an AI software-engineering assistant named Devin, by Cognition, working from the team's requirements, design reference, and decisions.

Factors considered

The development of LUNA was shaped by a commitment to scientific rigor, relying on established theories validated against NASA/JPL Horizons and textbook orbital mechanics, alongside primary datasets from NASA, JAXA, IAU/USGS, and JPL that include scripts for full auditing and rebuilding. The platform remains transparent about its limitations by stating dataset resolutions and model assumptions rather than inventing precision, while maintaining high performance through background-threaded searches, prioritized map tile caching, and shared Sun/Earth/Moon position calculations so the screen never freezes. Designed for intuitive usability across students, the curious public, and technical users, it keeps the Moon as the visual focus with movable panels, click-based interactions, plain-sentence result explanations, and an optional educational layer.

Bilingual support in English and Spanish is managed via dictionaries checked automatically before release, and the system functions seamlessly offline using a bundled base map whenever NASA's image service is unreachable. Built for long-term extensibility, maintainability, and privacy, LUNA allows future features like rover routes or trajectories to be added as small modules without a redesign, backed by typed code, 76 automated tests, pinned dependencies, and zero user tracking or accounts—keeping saved sites strictly in the user's browser. Finally, while a formal accessibility audit is still pending, the interface already accommodates diverse devices and needs through labeled controls, arrow-key timeline navigation, a high-contrast dark theme, and responsive layouts for desktop, tablet, and phone screens.
